methodology: M-W etymology pattern analysis with family breakdown comparison

action.mwEtymology: Latin actiōn-, actiō (from agere 'to drive, do' + -tiōn, -tiō nominalization suffix)

morphemeAnalysis.reasoning: ag is the root morpheme from agere; -tion is the nominalization suffix. M-W shows actiōn- (from actiō), which is ag + -tion. Perfect match.
morphemeAnalysis.notes: Surface form shows how Latin root appears in English compound. 'ag-' notation indicates root of agere.

nation.mwEtymology: Latin natiō, nātiōn- (from nasci 'to be born' + -tiōn, -tiō nominalization suffix)

morphemeAnalysis.reasoning: nat is the root stem from nasci (to be born); -ion is nominalization suffix. M-W nātiōn- (from natio) = nat + -tion. Note: -tion appears as -ion in Latin nominalization suffix form.
morphemeAnalysis.notes: This exemplifies Root allomorph pattern: nasci (infinitive) → nat (nominalization stem) → natio (nominalized form) → nation (English). Family correctly uses 'nat' stem.

production.mwEtymology: Latin productiōn-, productiō (from producere 'to lead forward/produce'; pro 'forward' + ducere 'to lead' + -tiōn nominalization)

morphemeAnalysis.reasoning: pro- is prefix (from pro 'forward'); duc is root from ducere (to lead); -tion is nominalization suffix. Family breakdown 'pro + duc + tion' perfectly matches M-W structure.
morphemeAnalysis.notes: Latin producere = pro + ducere, then nominalizes to productiō, then -tion in English. Three-morpheme structure: prefix + root + suffix.

education.mwEtymology: Latin educātiōn-, educātiō (from educāre 'to lead out, educate'; e/ex 'out' + ducāre intensive of ducere 'to lead' + -tiōn)

morphemeAnalysis.reasoning: e- is prefix from ex (out); duc is root; -ation is nominalization suffix. Latin educāre (from e + ducāre, intensive form of ducere). Family correctly shows e + duc + ation.
morphemeAnalysis.notes: Note ducāre is intensive form of ducere. In nominalization becomes educātiō. Family data doesn't specify 'intensive form' but structure is etymologically sound.

station.mwEtymology: Latin statiōn-, statiō (from stāre 'to stand' + -tiōn, -tiō nominalization suffix)

morphemeAnalysis.reasoning: M-W shows statiō from stāre (to stand). The stem 'stat-' comes from stāre (though this is complex: stāre → stai- in some forms → stat- in nominalization). Family shows 'stand' as root, which is correct conceptually (English cognate of stāre), but surface form is unclear.
morphemeAnalysis.notes: Root allomorph issue: stāre (infinitive) has different stem forms in different contexts. Nominalization uses stat- stem. Family notation 's + tation' or 'sta + tion' is ambiguous. Should be: stā/stat root + -tion suffix. Need to verify how family represents this.

traction.mwEtymology: Latin tractiōn-, tractiō (from trahere 'to draw, pull' + -tiōn nominalization suffix); root appears as tract- in nominalization stem

morphemeAnalysis.reasoning: tract- is the nominalization stem of trahere (to pull/draw). Latin tractiō uses tract + -tion. Family correctly shows 'tract + ion'. Note family lists 'tractare' (intensive form of trahere) as the root.
morphemeAnalysis.notes: This is a nominalized root allomorph: trahere (infinitive) → tract- (nominalization stem) → tractiō (nominalized form) → traction (English). Family structure correct.

abstraction.mwEtymology: Late Latin abstractiōn-, abstractiō (from abstrahere 'to pull away'; ab- 'away' + strahere variant of trahere 'to draw' + -tiōn)

morphemeAnalysis.reasoning: ab- is prefix (away); tract- is nominalization stem from trahere/strahere (to pull); -tion is suffix. M-W abstractiō = ab + str- (variant of tract-) + -tion. Family shows 'abs + tract + ion' where 'abs' captures ab + s (assimilation in Latin).
morphemeAnalysis.notes: Family notation 'abs' shows Latin phonetic form where ab + tract → abs + tract (b before t assimilates). Correctly represents Latin nominalization pattern.

inspection.mwEtymology: Latin inspectio, inspectionem (from inspicere 'to look at, inspect'; in- 'in, upon' + specere 'to look' + -tiōn)

morphemeAnalysis.reasoning: in- is prefix (in/upon); spec is nominalization stem from specere (to look); -tion is suffix. Latin inspectio (nominalized form from inspicere) = in + spect + -tion. Family breakdown correct.
morphemeAnalysis.notes: Specere root appears as 'spec-' in nominalization (specter, spectral also use spec-). Shows consistent allomorph pattern across this root family.

description.mwEtymology: Latin descriptio, descriptionem (from describere 'to write down, describe'; de- 'down' + scribere 'to write' + -tiōn)

morphemeAnalysis.reasoning: de- is prefix (down); scrib is root from scribere (to write); -tion is suffix. Latin descriptio (from describere) = de + script + -tion. Family breakdown correct.
morphemeAnalysis.notes: Scribere shows 'scrib-' in nominalization stem, consistent with 'script' in other derivatives (script, manuscript, etc.).

prescription.mwEtymology: Latin praescriptio, praescriptionem (from praescribere 'to write before, prescribe'; prae- 'before' + scribere 'to write' + -tiōn)

morphemeAnalysis.reasoning: pre- is prefix (from prae 'before'); scrib is root from scribere (to write); -tion is suffix. Latin praescriptio (from praescribere) = prae + script + -tion. Family shows 'pre' (English form of prae) + 'scrib + tion'.
morphemeAnalysis.notes: Prefix appears in English form ('pre-' not 'prae-'). This is normal: Latin prae → English pre in compound forms.

conversion.mwEtymology: Latin conversio, conversionem (from convertere 'to turn around, convert'; con- 'with, together' + vertere 'to turn' + -tiōn)

morphemeAnalysis.reasoning: con- is prefix (with/together); vers is nominalization stem from vertere (to turn); -ion is suffix (variant of -tion). Latin conversio (from convertere) = con + vers + -ion. Family breakdown correct.
morphemeAnalysis.notes: Note: -tion appears as -sion in Latin nominalization of vertere-family words. This is a morphological detail: vers + -io → version (not vertion).

version.mwEtymology: Latin versio, versionem (from vertere 'to turn'; literally 'a turning'). Root appears as vers- in nominalization stem.

morphemeAnalysis.reasoning: vers is nominalization stem from vertere (to turn); -ion is nominalization suffix. Latin versio = vers + -io (which becomes -ion in English). Family breakdown correct.
morphemeAnalysis.notes: Base nominalization without prefix (cf. conversion, diversion, etc.). Shows how root allomorph vers- appears in nominalized forms.

diversion.mwEtymology: Latin diversio, diversionem (from divertere 'to turn aside, divert'; di- variant of dis- 'apart' + vertere 'to turn' + -tiōn)

morphemeAnalysis.reasoning: di- (from dis-) is prefix (apart); vers is nominalization stem from vertere; -ion is suffix. Latin diversio (from divertere) = di(s) + vers + -ion. Family breakdown correct.
morphemeAnalysis.notes: Prefix shows as 'di-' in English (from Latin dis- which reduces before consonants to di-). This is regular Latin phonology.

mission.mwEtymology: Latin missio, missionem (from mittere 'to send, let go' + -tiōn nominalization suffix). Root appears as miss- in nominalization stem.

morphemeAnalysis.reasoning: miss is nominalization stem from mittere (to send); -ion is nominalization suffix. Latin missio = miss + -io (becomes -ion in English). Family breakdown correct.
morphemeAnalysis.notes: Note: mit is infinitive stem, miss- is nominalization stem. Family should reflect this as 'miss + ion' is correct.

emission.mwEtymology: Latin emissio, emissionem (from emittere 'to send out'; e- from ex- 'out' + mittere 'to send' + -tiōn)

morphemeAnalysis.reasoning: e- is prefix (from ex- 'out'); miss is nominalization stem from mittere (to send); -ion is suffix. Latin emissio = e + miss + -ion. Family breakdown correct.
morphemeAnalysis.notes: Prefix appears as 'e-' in English (from Latin ex- which reduces before consonants). Shows prefix + nominalized root + suffix pattern.

transmission.mwEtymology: Latin transmissio, transmissionem (from transmittere 'to send across'; trans- 'across' + mittere 'to send' + -tiōn)

morphemeAnalysis.reasoning: trans- is prefix (across); miss is nominalization stem from mittere; -ion is suffix. Latin transmissio (from transmittere) = trans + miss + -ion. Family breakdown correct.
morphemeAnalysis.notes: Multi-syllable prefix (trans-) + nominalized root + suffix pattern. Consistent with prefix + root + nominalization structure.

satisfaction.mwEtymology: Latin satisfactio, satisfactionem (from satisfacere 'to do enough'; satis 'enough' + facere 'to do, make' + -tiōn)

morphemeAnalysis.reasoning: satis (meaning 'enough') functions as prefix; fact is nominalization stem from facere (to make/do); -ion is suffix. Latin satisfactio = satis + fact + -ion. Family breakdown is correct with satis as prefix element.
morphemeAnalysis.notes: Complex case: satis is an adverb/prefix meaning 'enough' that becomes prefix in compounds. Nominalization uses fact- stem from facere. Shows how adverbial elements can function as prefixes.

competition.mwEtymology: Latin competitio, competitionem (from competere 'to meet together, compete'; com- 'together' + petere 'to strive, seek' + -tiōn)

morphemeAnalysis.reasoning: com- is prefix (together); pet is from petere (to strive/seek), but nominalization stem might be petit- (giving -tition ending, not -tion). Need to verify if family shows 'pet + ition' correctly or should be 'petit + ion'.
morphemeAnalysis.notes: Note ending: competition ends in -tition not -tion. This suggests nominalization stem petit- + -ion = -tition. Family shows 'com + pet + ition' which may need to be 'com + petit + ion' to show the nominalization stem properly.

pattern_1.name: Nominalized root allomorphs
pattern_1.description: Latin roots have different stems depending on context: infinitive vs nominalization
pattern_1.implication: Family data must show nominalization stem form (tract, stat, ag, miss, vers) not just infinitive stem

pattern_2.name: Prefix reduction before consonants
pattern_2.description: Latin prefixes reduce forms before certain consonants
examples: ab + strahere → as + trahere (assimilation, written as abstraction but parsed as ab + s-)
ex → e before consonants (emission from ex + mittere)
dis → di before certain consonants (diversion from dis + vertere)
pattern_2.implication: Family data may need to show reduced forms (abs, e, di) or note these phonological changes

pattern_3.name: Suffix variants in nominalization
pattern_3.description: -tion and -ion are variants of same nominalization suffix
pattern_3.implication: Suffix ID should capture that -tion, -sion, -ction are all nominalization (-ion) suffix variants

pattern_4.name: Complex prefixes functioning as semantic elements
pattern_4.description: Some prefix-like elements are words (satis 'enough') that become prefixes in compounds
examples: These are meaningful semantic units, not just morphosyntactic prefixes
pattern_4.implication: Prefix analysis should note semantic role (satis = 'enough' prefix meaning 'sufficiently')
